name: Erik Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run two CNC lathes at Varga Precision, a shop of about thirty people in an old railway shed. CNC means the lathe is controlled by a computer program, so I load the bar stock, set the tools, run the first part, measure it with the micrometer, tweak the offsets and then keep it running. We make hydraulic fittings mostly, brass and steel, thousands a week. I like the measuring part, getting a part to within a hundredth of a millimetre feels good. The boring part is standing there for hours while it just spins.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you fill those hours?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, I'm on my phone a lot, asking the AI stuff. I get it to check my programs, explain error codes, translate the German manual for the older lathe. I built a little spreadsheet for tool wear with it that the foreman now uses. Jo, my partner, is in her second year of nursing, so I'm basically paying for both of us on a wage that's not great, and we've got maybe a week or two saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, to be honest, I like this stuff. But I'd also say to the guys, see, nobody's coming for your lathe. Online I'd probably post a joke about how the AI still can't fix the coolant pump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I keep using the AI as a handy helper and that's it. The robot programming course I've been doing at night would be less useful than I hoped. I'd still be on low pay in a shop with no union, which is the real problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the course anyway, because Varga might buy a robot loader eventually and I want to be the one who runs it. I'd keep talking to the others about joining a union, which nobody likes hearing. Money-wise I'd just keep our heads above water until Jo qualifies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little flat, like a party got cancelled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the lack of a union is the real problem. Why hasn't one started?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of the guys think unions are for big plants. Old Pete says the last time someone tried, they got moved to nights. I've printed stuff off and left it in the break room twice. It keeps vanishing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when Jo qualifies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then there are two wages and we might actually save something. That's the plan, two more years of living on rice and the cheap coffee, then breathe. AI or no AI, that's what matters most at home.

S0.say: He'd admit he's a bit disappointed, but tell colleagues nobody is coming for their lathes. Online he'd joke that AI still can't fix the coolant pump.
S0.think: He'd keep using AI as a helper, and his night course in robot programming would be less useful than hoped. He sees low pay and no union as the real problem.
S0.do: Continues the robot programming course in case Varga buys a robot loader and keeps trying to interest colleagues in a union. Keeps the household afloat until his partner qualifies as a nurse.
S0.feel: Calm, but a little flat, like a cancelled party.
S0.quote: I've printed stuff off and left it in the break room twice. It keeps vanishing.
S0.fieldNote: Erik is unusual in being mildly disappointed that AI might not change much. He already uses AI daily and has built a tool his foreman uses. His real frustration is the lack of a union, and the leaflets that keep vanishing say a lot about the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is our chance, if we organise. If robots come in, someone has to program them and fix them, and that should be us, with a pay rise for the skill. Online I'd share stuff about workers getting a say in how tech comes in, like they do in some countries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd do alright, maybe better than now. I already speak the language, sort of. But I'd feel bad, because I can see Pete and Mo being the ones who get let go, and I'd be the guy who helped set up the thing that replaced them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the robot course by spring and ask the owner straight out to put me on any new cell. I'd push for a union or at least a works committee, so the training goes to everyone, not just me. If Varga wouldn't pay me more for it, I'd look at the bigger plant an hour away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and guilty at the same time. And a bit nervous, because we have no money if it goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd feel guilty about Pete and Mo. What would you actually do for them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teach them, if they'll let me. Mo's quick, he'd get it. Pete's sixty-one and says he'd rather sweep floors than learn a tablet. I can't force that, but I can make sure the company has to offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would moving to the bigger plant be realistic with Jo's studies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd be a long commute in my old car, an hour each way. Fuel would eat a chunk of any raise. So it's more of a threat I'd use than a plan I'd love.

S1.say: He'd call it a chance if workers organise, arguing that operators should program and fix the new robots and be paid for it. Online he'd share material on giving workers a say over new technology.
S1.think: He believes he'd do alright, maybe better than now, as he already understands the tools. But he'd feel guilty about older colleagues being let go while he helped install their replacements.
S1.do: Finishes his robot course by spring and asks to be put on any new cell. Pushes for a union or works committee so training is shared, and considers the larger plant an hour away if Varga won't pay more.
S1.feel: Excited and guilty at once, with nerves because there's no money if it goes wrong.
S1.quote: I'd be the guy who helped set up the thing that replaced them.
S1.fieldNote: Erik is the rare person who sees himself winning from automation and feels guilty about it. His progressive politics show up as wanting training shared with everyone. The thin cushion is the only thing that makes him nervous here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has to be handled by everyone, not by companies one at a time. Public ownership of the big AI systems, a basic income, now, not in five years. I'd be loud online, probably louder than is good for me at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my whole plan breaks. Learning to program robots is pointless if the AI programs the robots. I'd be just as out of work as Pete, only two years later, maybe less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still try to be the last human on the floor, the one who checks the robots and signs things off, for as long as that lasts. I'd use AI to look for anything, gig work, remote stuff, even teaching others to use it. Jo and I would cut back hard, and we'd probably lean on her parents so she can finish her degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground I was standing on, the bit I thought was safe, is the bit that's sinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years' warning, does being adaptive help you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd move fast while others are still arguing about whether it's real. But being fast doesn't help much when the finish line is that the job doesn't exist. I'd just get to the end quicker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jo that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That at least nurses are hands and heart, so maybe she lasts longer. Then I'd look at her face and know she's thinking the same thing about robots in hospitals. We'd probably just sit on the sofa and not say much.

S2.say: He'd argue the change must be handled collectively, calling for public ownership of big AI systems and a basic income immediately. He'd be loud online, possibly risking trouble at work.
S2.think: He sees his whole plan collapse, since learning to program robots is pointless if AI does it. He expects to be as jobless as older colleagues, just a little later.
S2.do: Tries to stay on as the person who checks robots and signs off work as long as possible, while using AI to hunt for any income. Cuts back hard and leans on Jo's parents so she can finish her degree.
S2.feel: Like the ground he thought was safe is the part that's sinking.
S2.quote: Being fast doesn't help much when the finish line is that the job doesn't exist. I'd just get to the end quicker.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI flips Erik's advantage: the skill he's been building becomes the thing that gets automated. He still moved quickly in his plans, but without hope. The quiet sofa moment with Jo was the most emotional thing he said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to set up a real safety net, if governments start now. I'd be pushing for people like me to get a share, a stake in the machines that replace us. I'd talk about it at work, even if Pete rolls his eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years gives me a window where my skills are worth a lot. Firms will need people to install and run robots for a while before the AI does it all. I could make good money for three or four years, if I'm smart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the course, then get certified on one big robot brand within a year, and move to a plant that's installing them, even with the commute. I'd save every bit of the extra money, not upgrade anything. And I'd keep pushing the union idea wherever I end up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but switched on. Like a race where I at least know where the start line is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with three or four years of better money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay off the car, build a proper cushion, help Jo through her last year without her doing so many night shifts at the supermarket. Maybe put a bit into one of those worker co-op funds, if they exist by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Varga?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mo, honestly. He's thirty, two kids, and he's good but he doesn't trust computers. If I left for the bigger plant, I'd want to drag him along with me.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough for a real safety net if governments act now, and he'd push for workers to get a stake in the machines replacing them. He'd talk about it at work despite eye-rolls.
S3.think: He sees a window of three or four years where installing and running robots pays well before AI takes that over. He thinks he could earn good money if he's smart.
S3.do: Completes his course, gets certified on a major robot brand within a year and moves to a plant installing them. Saves all the extra pay and keeps pushing for a union at his new workplace.
S3.feel: Nervous but switched on, like knowing where the start line is.
S3.quote: Five years gives me a window where my skills are worth a lot.
S3.fieldNote: Erik treats the five-year version as a window to earn and save before the end point. He wants to bring his colleague Mo with him. He is honest that the window is temporary but sounded more energised than in the fast scenario.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to rebuild how work and money are shared. Shorter weeks, shared ownership, a public stake in AI. I'd probably get involved properly, maybe stand for something at the union or the council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd come out of it okay for most of the decade. I'm the kind of person who'll be early. What scares me is year eleven, when even the robot people aren't needed, and whether society has sorted itself out by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the five-year one, I'd retrain and move toward robot work, but I'd also take a longer course, maybe a two-year technical diploma in automation, at night. Jo would be working by then, so we'd save properly. I'd want to be on some workers' committee shaping how the machines come in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful, with a knot somewhere at the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd come out okay, but also that year eleven scares you. Which is stronger?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Day to day, the hope. At three in the morning, the knot. I think both are true, and I'd rather plan for the hope and campaign about the knot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change any family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd maybe have a kid around thirty-two, once Jo's settled. Ten years feels like enough time to make a life, even if nobody knows what the world looks like after.

S4.say: He'd argue ten years is enough to rebuild how work and money are shared, through shorter weeks, shared ownership and a public stake in AI. He might stand for a role in the union or the council.
S4.think: He expects to do well for most of the decade because he moves early. What scares him is the year after, when even robot specialists aren't needed, and whether society has adapted.
S4.do: Retrains towards robot work and takes a two-year technical diploma in automation at night. Saves properly once Jo is working and joins a workers' committee on how machines are introduced.
S4.feel: Mostly hopeful, with a knot at the back.
S4.quote: Day to day, the hope. At three in the morning, the knot.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Erik's mood lifts and his politics become a plan to get involved. He clearly separates his own decade, which looks good, from the end point, which worries him. He'd still start a family, which says a lot about his confidence.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it wipes out the one advantage I have, being early. What would help is a basic income that doesn't depend on a job, and some public share in the AI systems so the money doesn't all go to a few companies. And for shops like Varga, real help for workers to organise.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask whether people want this. I like the tech, I really do. But nobody at Varga was asked if they wanted robots, and I think that's half of why Pete hates them.

headlineQuote: Learning to program robots is pointless if the AI programs the robots.
portrait: Erik is a 27-year-old CNC lathe operator at a thirty-person precision shop in an old railway shed, supporting his partner Jo through nursing school on low pay and a week or two of savings. He uses AI every day and is studying robot programming at night, so he is one of the few who sees automation as a chance for himself. His progressive politics show up as guilt about older colleagues and a push for unions, shared training and public ownership. The fast AGI scenario hits him hardest because it erases his advantage of being early, while the ten-year version leaves him mostly hopeful but worried about what comes after.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it wipes out his one advantage, being early.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income not tied to a job, a public share in AI systems, and real help for workers in small shops to organise.
